blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: SEBI was given statutory powers on April 12, 1992, under the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992.
The functions of SEBI are broadly categorized into three heads: Regulatory Functions, Protective Functions, and Developmental Functions.
Regulatory functions involve registering and regulating brokers, sub-brokers, share transfer agents, collective investment schemes, and mutual funds.
Protective functions focus on controlling insider trading, prohibiting price rigging, and preventing fraudulent and unfair trade practices.
Developmental functions emphasize training intermediaries, conducting investor education programs, and promoting flexible market practices.

blocks.content: • Registers brokers, merchant bankers, portfolio managers, and credit rating agencies.
The primary objective of SEBI is to protect the interests of investors in securities and to promote the development of and regulate the securities market.
• Regulates mutual funds and collective investment schemes.

rows: Protect investor interests and prevent market malpractices
Prohibiting price rigging, stopping insider trading, promoting fair conduct, investor education
Regulate and maintain order in the financial market operations
Registering brokers and mutual funds, auditing stock exchanges, regulating takeovers
Expand market scope, adopt modern techniques, and train stakeholders
Training market intermediaries, promoting internet trading, encouraging self-regulatory organizations

blocks.content: • Prevents fraudulent and unfair trade practices.

items: Distinction Alert: Prohibition of insider trading and price rigging fall under Protective Functions, not Regulatory Functions.
Timeline Alert: SEBI was initially set up as a non-statutory body in 1988 before gaining statutory status in 1992.
Registration of stockbrokers, merchant bankers, and mutual funds is classified under Regulatory Functions.
